Body Changes

Your body belongs to you: this story builds correct body-part vocabulary, growing body awareness, and the confidence to decide who gets to touch it.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

At bath time, your child suddenly asks why their body looks different from their sister's or their desk neighbour's. In the changing room, kids compare themselves, whisper, giggle over words they've picked up but don't really understand. For you as a parent, a very practical uncertainty often surfaces: which words do I use? How much do I explain? And how do I teach my child that their body belongs to them, without making the topic bigger or more shameful than it needs to be?

At this age, a child's body genuinely starts to change, or at least becomes a topic because other children are further along or not yet there. At the same time, awareness of privacy grows: things that used to happen in front of everyone without a second thought suddenly feel uncomfortable. Children this age also understand, far more clearly than younger ones, that there's a difference between a touch that feels good and one that doesn't — but they need the language and the confidence to actually say no.

A story makes a topic discussable that many families would rather avoid. Through a character asking the same questions about their own body, feeling the same shyness while getting changed, the conversation loosens up — your child's own questions suddenly feel less embarrassing, because someone else has already asked them. Your child also sees a character clearly saying no when a touch feels wrong, and rehearses that no internally before it's ever needed in real life.

In the personalized story, your child — with their own face on every page — learns correct words for their body, discovers that every body is different and still right, and practices the core rule: your own body belongs to you, and you're allowed to say no. The story stays factual and age-appropriate throughout, without going into unnecessary detail. The first story is free, so you can read it in advance and decide how you want to approach the topic together.

For home: use correct anatomical terms from the start rather than pet names — this also protects your child, because in a serious situation they can describe clearly what happened. Answer questions briefly and factually, as much as is asked and no more. Practice together saying no loudly and walking away when a touch feels wrong — including with familiar people like relatives. And if your child reacts unusually strongly to touch, suddenly withdraws, or hints at some kind of assault, contact your paediatrician or a specialist service such as a victim support centre right away.

What your child learns

Body knowledge, correct vocabulary, bodily autonomy, setting boundaries, saying no.

Recommended age

6-11 years

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the right words to use for private body parts?

Use the correct anatomical terms rather than pet names, from as early as possible. This isn't about being clinical — it protects your child, because clear language means they can describe exactly what happened if something ever feels wrong, and adults can take them seriously right away.

At what age should I start talking about bodily boundaries?

Much earlier than most parents think — even toddlers can learn that they decide who hugs or kisses them. Around school age, this can be extended into clearer rules about private body parts and the right to say no to anyone, including family members.

My child is embarrassed to talk about body changes — how do I open the conversation?

Bring it up in relaxed, everyday moments rather than a big formal talk — during bath time, in the car, or through a book that raises the same questions indirectly. Keep your own tone matter-of-fact; children pick up on embarrassment from adults just as much as they carry their own.

Is it normal for children to compare bodies at this age?

Yes, this is a completely normal part of developing body awareness, especially once differences between children become more visible. Use it as an opening to talk about how bodies develop at different paces and all count as normal, rather than treating the comparing itself as a problem.

What warning signs should make me seek professional help?

Take note if your child suddenly avoids being touched, shows unusual knowledge or behaviour beyond their age, becomes fearful of a specific person, or hints at something happening without being able to say it directly. In any of these cases, contact your paediatrician or a specialised victim support service without delay — they are trained to ask the right questions calmly.
